newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY SAYS SLOVAK LANGUAGE LAW DELAY BREAKS TREATY.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY SAYS SLOVAK LANGUAGE LAW DELAY BREAKS TREATY.

text.p: Hungary on Monday appealed to Slovakia to pass a long-awaited minority language law, saying Bratislava was contravening its international commitments to its ethnic Hungarian minority by delaying the legislation.
The law is a requirement of the basic treaty ratified by Hungary and Slovakia last year which guarantees current borders, human rights, and the protection of minorities.
"The present day situation is against the spirit and the word of the basic treaty," Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs told Reuters in an interview.

"Slovak politicians up to the highest level have promised repeatedly to the Hungarian minority in Slovakia...and to the politicians and experts on the Council of Europe that they would solve the issue of the use of minority languages -- so far they have failed to keep their promises."

The Slovak government, led by Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, provoked international condemenation by introducing a controversial language law late in 1995 making Slovak the only language to be used in public places.

However, it also promised to pass a law protecting minority languages but has so far failed to put the bill before parliament, provoking strong criticism from Slovak Presoident Michal Kovac as well as the Council of Europe and the United States.
Kovacs said he had suggested to his Slovak counterpart that all that was necessary was to bring together existing legislation.

"My argument when we last discussed the issue was that if you have in Slovakia some dozens of laws on the use of the minority language, what is your argument against having just one bill which would incorporate all this legisalation into one?"

Kovacs also confirmed that the two countries were exploring ways of reaching an out-of-court settlement of the current Gabcikovo dam dispute, under which Slovakia has diverted waters from the Danube to a hydro-electric project.

The construction had originally been a joint venture between the communist governments of Hungary and the then Czechoslovakia but Hungary unilaterally pulled out in 1989 citing environmental concerns, while newly-created Slovakia decided to go it alone.
Slovakia is claiming damages from Hungary for breach of contract while Hungary complains the dam is causing environmental damage.
